intro: By the time I was born in 2007, the internet in the United States was already shifting from a dial-up curiosity into something households were beginning to treat as a utility. Home broadband had only crossed the 50% mark of American adults in early 2006, and cable and DSL companies were racing each other for the newly broadband-curious.

This page covers the years right around my birth, when 'getting online' stopped meaning a screeching modem handshake and started meaning an always-on cable or DSL line, and when the first wave of social platforms (Facebook, YouTube, Twitter) were opening their doors to the public.

events.headline: Broadband crosses the tipping point
events.detail: By March 2006, 42% of American adults (about 84 million people) had broadband at home, up from 30% a year earlier — a 40% jump in twelve months. Price cuts by cable and DSL providers were the main driver.
events.sourceName: Pew Research Center, "Broadband Adoption in the United States" (2006)

events.headline: Facebook opens to everyone
events.detail: Facebook, founded in 2004 for university students, removed its membership restrictions in September 2006 and let anyone with an email address sign up, turning a campus network into a mass platform.
events.sourceName: HubSpot, "The History of Social Media Since 2003"

events.headline: Twitter launches
events.detail: Jack Dorsey, Evan Williams and Biz Stone launched Twitter on March 21, 2006, introducing short-form 'microblogging' as a new way to follow real-time events and conversations.

events.headline: The rural-urban broadband gap becomes visible
events.detail: Around this time, only about 31% of rural Americans had broadband at home compared with 47% of the population overall — an early sign of the 'digital divide' that would shape US broadband policy for the next two decades.

events.headline: The 2007–2009 housing crisis slows (but doesn't stop) broadband growth
events.detail: The US housing bust cut broadband 'net adds' roughly in half compared with the 10-million-plus added annually in 2005–2006, as new home construction and house moves (a common trigger for signing up to a provider) collapsed. Growth continued, just more slowly.
events.sourceName: S&P Global Market Intelligence, "The History of US Broadband"

events.headline: 68% of the US has home broadband
events.detail: By the end of the decade, 68% of the US population had some form of broadband internet service at home — DSL, cable, or increasingly, fibre services like Verizon FiOS — up from well under half just five years earlier.
events.sourceName: National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), "Exploring the Digital Nation" (2010)
